catalog_quote: Stress is assigned to the root-final syllable of a word. Examples of stress assignment to the root-final syllable are provided for verbs and nouns in (7-8) and (9-10), respectively. In nouns, this stress pattern is a bit obscured as they always surface with the extrametrical nominalizing enclitic =a. On the surface, then, stress falls on the penultimate syllable of nouns bearing the enclitic =a. (7) /ɛ-pi/ → [ɛ.ˈpi] 2.sg.imp-shut.off ‘Shut off!’ (8) /ɛ-kɨtʃi/ → [ɛ.kɨ.ˈtʃi] 2.sg.imp-cut ‘Cut (it)!’ (9) /janu=a/ → [ñã.ˈndu.a] spider=nmlz ‘spider’ (10) /tapiPiR=a/ → [ta.pi.ˈPi.Ra] tapir=nmlz ‘tapir’ However, some suffixes trigger stress shift from the root-final syllable, both in verbs and nouns. new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the last syllable of the root; the nominalizer enclitic =a and the negation suffix -i are unstressed (so =a-nouns are surface-penultimate), while a small set of suffixes (-ahim 'very', -uhu 'aug', -ʔi 'dim') take the stress themselves. In unsuffixed words this is word-final stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed by dos Santos 2024 (only primary stress marked). For the sister dialect Júma, Abrahamson & Abrahamson 1984 report alternating stresses counting leftward from the final syllable.
new_statements.exceptions: Extrametrical =a (nouns surface penultimate: [ta.pi.ˈʔi.ɾa] 'tapir'); stress-attracting suffixes -ahim, -uhu, -ʔi (e.g. [aĩmbɛ-aˈhĩm] 'be very sharp', [vɨɾaˈʔia] 'small bird'); negation nd-..-i does not shift stress ([nd-aĩˈmbɛ-i] 'be dull').
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress in citation/elicited forms; the analysis is explicitly based on the Juma (juma1249) and Jupaú/Uru-Eu-Wau-Wau (urue1240) dialects of what the author treats as one language, Kawahíva, of which Karipuna (kari1317) is a dialect. No Karipuna forms are used in the stress section.
new_statements.identity_note: kari1317 'Karipúna' here = the Kawahíb-speaking Karipuna de Rondônia (T.I. Karipuna, Jaci-Paraná; self-designation ahé), NOT Karipuna do Amapá (Creole French kmv) nor the older Panoan 'Karipuna/Jau-Navo' (Glottolog's own comment flags this Ethnologue confusion; the Australian items in the supplied glottolog_refs list are spurious). The quoted stress statement is dos Santos 2024's for 'Kawahíva' as a single language of eight dialects that explicitly includes Karipuna (Table 2.4 lists kari1317/kuq), but his phonology is 'based on the Juma [juma1249] and Jupaú [urue1240] dialects'; no Karipuna forms appear in the stress section. Concordant root-final/final statements exist for sister dialects Tenharim/Jiahui/Amondawa (Marçoli 2018) and Júma (Abrahamson & Abrahamson 1984). A Karipuna-specific statement would require Ferreira & Ferreira 1992 (USP ms.) or Sampaio 2001 (UNIR PhD).

sources.note: Sec. 3.2.1, printed p.40 (PDF p.57): 'Stress is assigned to the root-final syllable of a word.' Nouns surface with penultimate stress because the nominalizing enclitic =a is extrametrical; negation circumfix nd-..-i leaves stress on the root; suffixes -ahim 'very', -uhu 'aug', -ʔi 'dim' attract stress (pp.40-41). Also p.38: oral/nasal vowel contrast restricted to the root-final syllable 'which coincides with the location of stress'. sources.note: Sister dialect Júma: sec. 5 Tonicidade 'O acento mais forte recai na última sílaba da palavra', alternating secondary stresses leftward, listed exceptions (final V syllable, -an, some -ma/-na/-ŋa words, cliticized postpositions/pronouns). Same SIL team wrote the unpublished 1980 'Karipuna and Júma comparative study'.

sources.note: Pan-dialect Kawahíb dictionary with Karipuna data (fieldwork 15 Apr-2 May 1980, FUNAI Posto Panorama, Jaci Paraná; entries labelled 'K'). Introduction sec. 2 'Phonetic Symbols' (pp.2-4) gives segment values and nasalization rules but no stress rule; the only stress remark is incidental, in the Parintintin grammar overview p.7: 'In one syllable reduplication the final stressed syllable is reduplicated' (presupposes final stress, Parintintin). No Karipuna-specific stress/accent note anywhere (a full-text search for stress/accent/tonic).
